name: Floral ceramic dish — course cover

sections.Form & Surface: A shallow circular ceramic dish has a glossy white surface and a narrow red-edged rim. A double red circle encloses the central flower group.
sections.Composition: The centre presents the flowers upright. The outer groups rotate around it. The circular frame makes the same floral vocabulary work at two scales: a small central arrangement and an enlarged surrounding repeat.
sections.Colour & Motifs: Two upright red flowers with dark blue bases fill the centre, among green leaves and slender flowering stems. Three large blue-and-red flower groups turn around the outer field. Green leaves, looping red stems and small rosettes fill the spaces between them.

name: Floral fabric detail — course cover

sections.Field & Border Organization: Two decorated panels flank a pale vertical strip. Red outer edges enclose cream floral borders, dark green upper fields and red lower fields. The borders follow the panels’ curved and angled edges.
sections.Colour & Motifs: Red flowers and long-tailed birds occupy the green fields. Gold-coloured linework outlines curling stems, leaves, petals and wings. Small red flowers repeat along the cream borders. Blue flowers appear in the lower red field.
sections.Composition: The pale centre separates the paired patterned panels. Dense small-scale stems and flowers contrast with the dish’s larger, widely spaced floral forms above.

name: Trader with horses — Mahanabami Dibba relief

sections.Pose & Gesture: The figure bends both arms outward toward the horses. A long garment falls toward the lower edge, and a pointed head covering rises above the face. The figures share a shallow horizontal ground.
sections.Material & Technique: The scene is carved in low relief on grainy stone. Cut outlines separate the horses’ heads, necks and legs from the background. The bodies project from the flat surrounding surface.
sections.Subject & Composition: A standing figure occupies the centre between two inward-facing horses. The horses’ heads turn toward the figure, making the handler the point where the two halves of the panel meet.
sections.Course Identification: Course reading: The index identifies the panel as a trader with horses from the Mahanabami Dibba at Hampi. Its return on slide 16 places the horse trader beside steel and textiles under ‘Trade connections’. Slide 25 returns it to the module’s cultural/trade recap.

headings: Phases of Development of the Platform
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The early granite carving and later green-chlorite facing are placed together as phases of the Mahanabami Dibba. Differences in surface, cutting and figural handling are read historically within one monument. The preceding memorial comparison supplies a stylistic reference; the following horse-trade slide shifts attention to the people and goods represented.

headings: Mahanabami Dibba and Cultural/Trade Connections
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The royal platform, horse trader, hero stone and warrior recap the module’s cultural/trade argument. Ceremony, commerce, commemoration and martial imagery contribute different evidence. Their grouping joins social and political functions to travelling forms; it does not reduce Hampi’s art to one exclusively religious or decorative meaning.

name: Golconda Coverlet — central pavilion

sections.Field & Border Organization: A central multi-tiered pavilion divides a roughly square field. A seated figure is beneath its canopy. Standing attendants and birds occupy the sides and upper corners. Several narrow patterned borders frame the field.
sections.Dyes & Materials: Red, green, dark outlines and a pale ground organize the design.
sections.Function: Course reading: Captioned coverlet. The architecture belongs to the depicted scene rather than the textile’s physical support.
sections.Circulation: Course reading: The identical pavilion, seated pair, surrounding figures and borders establish the cross-module image match. Module 2 provides National Museum accession 48.7-103.
sections.Motifs & Locations:
Module 2 slide 14 enlarges the lower-left standing figures and a spiky fruit beside them.

Course reading: Its heading identifies pineapple.

The full view also contains birds above the roof and large flowering plants beside attendants.

headings: How do we differentiate these kalamkari works?
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Golconda coverlet is paired with the hanging of Manikkavachar and Meenakshi’s wedding. The heading asks how to differentiate kalamkari works, not how to treat them as one subject.

name: Lotus Mahal

sections.Building Type & Function: Course reading: Palatial pavilion in Hampi’s royal quarter.
sections.Plan & Spatial Organization: The diagram shows a central grid with projections on four sides. The section distinguishes two storeys and a higher central roof.
sections.Structural System:
Repeated cusped arches sit beneath horizontal eaves and stepped roof masses.

Course reading: The lecture compares this arcuate vocabulary with temple and palatial tower forms.
sections.Elevation & Massing: A dominant pyramidal central tower is surrounded by lower stepped towers. Deep overhanging eaves separate the levels.
sections.Ornament Vocabulary: Slide 24 reveals layered arch mouldings, lace-like scrollwork and a large mask-like face directly above the central cusp.
sections.Syncretism: Course reading: The lecture explicitly joins Hindu temple/palatial pyramidal forms with Islamic arch and stucco vocabularies in one structure.

headings: Ebb and Flow: Art and Globalism of Oceanic Networks
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The cover pairs a floral ceramic dish and floral fabric with a stone trader-and-horses relief under Ebb and Flow: Art and Globalism of Oceanic Networks. Repeated flowers connect ceramic and textile; the relief contributes the people and traded animals. This cross-media grouping argues for the circulation of goods, designs and artisanal knowledge through contact. The Paigah Tombs and Coromandel kalamkari hanging on slides 2–3 extend that argument into architectural ornament, textile making and human interaction.

occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Vijaya Vitthala warrior, Ascetic Riding a Nag and Père Tanguy form the final recap. name: Adoration of the Christ Child — Golconda

sections.Composition: The infant lies centrally in a cradle, surrounded by kneeling and standing figures. Airborne winged figures occupy the top. An elaborate blue-and-gold-coloured border encloses the dark floral field.
sections.Perspective Convention: The cradle is oblique but the figures are stacked in a shallow field rather than a unified Renaissance room.
sections.Figural Style: The woman beside the cradle and the infant have radiating halos. Several lower figures wear strongly patterned or contrasting local-looking clothes.
sections.Motifs & Hidden Details: Two hovering figures above carry objects or garlands. Another long-winged attendant stands behind the cradle. Vessels and offerings lie below. A row of small white waterbirds occupies the very bottom.
sections.Subject Matter vs Technique Origin: Course reading: Christian narrative appears in a Golconda painting with Persianate borders, textile-like ground and locally adapted figures.

name: Interior of Badshahi Ashurkhana

sections.Building Type & Function: Course reading: Ashurkhana interior in Hyderabad, a Shi‘i commemorative setting rather than an ordinary secular hall.
sections.Plan & Spatial Organization: A railing encloses the central display of standards. Suspended lamps and a chandelier hang between the foreground posts.
sections.Structural System: Visible posts support horizontal ceiling members. Painted or tiled pointed niches on the walls are not themselves proof of load-bearing arches.
sections.Ornament Vocabulary: Blue, green and gold-coloured tile fields, calligraphic ornament and pointed compartments cover the rear and side walls.
sections.Motifs & Locations:
Hand-shaped and round standards stand at the rear.

Course reading: They belong to the ritual furnishing, not the wall’s structural system.

name: Persianate cosmopolis

sections.Definition: Course reading: In the lecture’s use of Emma Flatt, Persianate culture involves shared language practice and political aesthetics across regions, while allowing exchange and conflict.
sections.Nearest Confusable Terms: Course reading: Persianate is broader than Persian nationality or manufacture in Iran. Shared practice does not imply one ethnicity, one religion or political harmony.
sections.Applied To: Course reading: Bijapur’s Siesta, travelling artists, Bidar’s madrasa and Deccani objects provide the module’s cases.

occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Persianate World / Persian Cosmopolis discussion uses Siesta to connect a Deccani scene with a wider courtly visual culture. The following madrasa comparison extends the enquiry from painting to architecture. Persianate connection is a framework for local adaptation, not a statement that every work was made in Iran.

name: A Vase with Flowers — Vosmaer

sections.Composition: A tall bouquet fills almost the whole panel above a metal-coloured handled vase. Blossoms turn in different directions, while isolated fallen petals and flowers rest on the stone ledge below.
sections.Perspective Convention: Overlapping blossoms create depth within a narrow frontal space. The vessel and ledge anchor the bouquet.
sections.Palette & Pigment: Striped yellow-red tulips, pink blossoms and a blue-white iris stand out against near-black foliage. These are colour observations.
sections.Line & Hand: Sharp petal edges and individually differentiated flower surfaces produce the naturalistic effect.
sections.Motifs & Hidden Details: A pale butterfly appears low in the bouquet near the central striped tulip. Drooping stems and detached flowers interrupt the apparent plenitude.

name: Ocean at the Table — commodities and still life

sections.Argument: Course reading: The module treats still life as an entry into maritime trade, material knowledge, wealth and artisanal labour. Its 1609–1713 Dutch Golden Age frame links overseas commerce with changes in Dutch society.
sections.Evidence & Artworks: Course reading: Vosmaer’s flowers, Vermeer’s maps and carpet, van Beyeren’s luxurious food, Dou’s manufactured objects, van Aelst’s armour and d’Hondecoeter’s animals provide different forms of evidence.
sections.Course Throughline: Course reading: Objects and organisms circulate with people and knowledge. A still life can therefore be studied beyond genre classification, while keeping the pictured object separate from the commodity’s documented origin.

headings: Ocean at the Table

sections.Palette & Pigment: Blue cloud forms, green landscape and bright orange-yellow drapery replace the monochrome tonal structure of the comparison engraving.
sections.Motifs & Hidden Details: Winged children and trumpet-playing angels float across the top. A skull and long bones occupy the foreground. Small pale and brown animals stand at lower right. A standing winged attendant appears on the right edge.

headings: European and Mughal Art Encounters: Derivative? Altered? Creative?

headings: Idea of Lineage or Silsila

name: Virgin and Child — Ghulam

sections.Composition: A seated mother with bent knees supports a twisting child within a mostly empty pale field, surrounded by a blue-and-gold-coloured scrolling border.
sections.Line & Hand: Fine dark outlines and restrained wash define folds, face and limbs. The limited colour makes drawing particularly prominent.
sections.Figural Style: The mother inclines her head and wears a veil and necklaces. Her seated posture spreads the drapery across the bottom.
sections.Text–Image Relationship: Small inscriptions appear at lower left of the figure. The slide reports that the work was made for Prince Salim.
sections.Subject Matter vs Technique Origin: Course reading: A Christian maternal theme is translated into a Mughal ink, opaque-watercolour and gold album image. Printed European imagery is part of the lecture’s explanation.

name: Globe in the Mughal Court

sections.Argument: Course reading: European prints, books and cartographic forms entered Mughal courtly image-making and were selectively adapted. The module asks how foreign visual resources became tools for local political and religious expression.
sections.Evidence & Artworks: Course reading: Christian-themed paintings, the Gulshan composite page, artists’ studies, and Jahangir’s two globe allegories show different mechanisms of transfer.
sections.Course Throughline: Course reading: Trade and travel move images and skills as well as goods. Indian-centred cartography and transformed religious imagery make the receiving court an active interpreter.

occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Mughal and Iranian animal carpets are placed within the question of continental and maritime trade. Their shared textile format supports comparison of animal imagery and production contexts across regions. The next muslin examples extend the enquiry from patterned furnishing to the material qualities of cloth.

headings: Sartorial choices and legitimacy of a ruler
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Akbar and Adham Khan is used to discuss sartorial choices and a ruler’s legitimacy after the muslin sequence. Clothing operates as a political visual language, not simply surface pattern. The following Christian-subject paintings extend the enquiry into the Mughal court’s selective use of different visual resources.

headings: Mughal depiction of Christian themes
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Basawan’s Virgin and Child is paired across adjacent slides with a work after Luini. The shared mother-and-child subject supports comparison of gesture, setting and modelling across Mughal and European images. The later date of the displayed Luini copy prevents treating that particular object as Basawan’s direct model.

headings: Making of the Mughal Atelier of Painting
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Akbar’s combat-of-ascetics scene and Leonardo’s Virgin of the Rocks place Mughal atelier practice beside European Renaissance composition. Crowded action and the contained devotional grouping provide different organizations of figures and space. The sequence broadens artistic encounter beyond a claim of simple copying.

headings: European and Mughal Art Encounters: Derivative? Altered? Creative?
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Mughal Deposition follows the church and European painting sequence under Derivative? Altered? Creative? The familiar Christian subject becomes a test of adaptation in figures, setting and handling. Slide 17 returns to it beside Raimondi’s print so that a broad encounter can be examined as a particular composition comparison.

headings: Classical texts of diverse traditions—including Indic, Islamicate, Persianate, Central Asian, and Greco-Roman—were collected, translated, and studied at the Mughal court
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Ghulam’s Virgin and Child sits within the discussion of collecting and studying classical texts from diverse traditions at the Mughal court. The image becomes a case of active selection and translation between pictorial worlds. The following Bihzad–Abd al-Samad comparison makes artistic lineage a more specific mechanism.

headings: Establishing Lineage and Connections through Art Styles
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Gulshan sheet assembles a Luna engraving with Persian drawings of a seated man, a group of men and a lion. The whole and its components must be read together: collecting, cutting, mounting and framing create a new relationship among previously separate images. One page therefore need not have one maker, date or original medium.

headings: Jahangir, King of the World, Globe and Territory
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The full Jahangir–Malik Ambar allegory and its details connect the emperor’s body to a mapped globe, cosmic supports and a defeated enemy. The India-centred globe is part of a political claim. Repeated enlargement trains attention to the small devices through which cartographic form becomes imperial imagery.

Christian-themed paintings, the Gulshan composite page, artists’ studies, and Jahangir’s two globe allegories show different mechanisms of transfer.
Trade and travel move images and skills as well as goods.
Indian-centred cartography and transformed religious imagery make the receiving court an active interpreter.

name: Occidentalism and Orientalism — lecture comparison

sections.Definition: Course reading: Slide 4 asks how a Mughal engagement with western images and styles differs from Orientalism. Occidentalism here is a working label for looking toward or representing the West. The slide poses a comparison rather than defining a complete theory.
sections.Nearest Confusable Terms: Course reading: Orientalism can name European artistic representations of the East and, in critical theory, systems of knowledge tied to unequal power. These meanings must be separated from a simple compass-direction reversal.
sections.Applied To: Course reading: Akbar and Adham Khan introduces the question. Christian adaptations and European print models provide the ensuing cases.

headings: Sartorial choices and legitimacy of a ruler
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Akbar and Adham Khan is used to discuss sartorial choices and a ruler’s legitimacy after the muslin sequence. Clothing operates as a political visual language, not simply surface pattern. The following Christian-subject paintings extend the enquiry into the Mughal court’s selective use of different visual resources.

headings: Mughal depiction of Christian themes
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Basawan’s Virgin and Child is paired across adjacent slides with a work after Luini. The shared mother-and-child subject supports comparison of gesture, setting and modelling across Mughal and European images. The later date of the displayed Luini copy prevents treating that particular object as Basawan’s direct model.

headings: European and Mughal Art Encounters: Derivative? Altered? Creative?
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Mughal Deposition follows the church and European painting sequence under Derivative? Altered? Creative? The familiar Christian subject becomes a test of adaptation in figures, setting and handling. Slide 17 returns to it beside Raimondi’s print so that a broad encounter can be examined as a particular composition comparison.

headings: Classical texts of diverse traditions—including Indic, Islamicate, Persianate, Central Asian, and Greco-Roman—were collected, translated, and studied at the Mughal court
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Ghulam’s Virgin and Child sits within the discussion of collecting and studying classical texts from diverse traditions at the Mughal court. The image becomes a case of active selection and translation between pictorial worlds. The following Bihzad–Abd al-Samad comparison makes artistic lineage a more specific mechanism.

headings: Idea of Lineage or Silsila
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The queried Dürer Crucifixion, Abu’l Hasan’s Saint John and Abdullah Khan’s hawking scene place European print study alongside Mughal portraiture and courtly activity. These examples belong to the lineage discussion while differing in subject and making process. A European religious figure supplies a visual resource, not the identity of every local patron.

headings: Idea of Lineage or Silsila
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Mughal Deposition is placed beside Raimondi’s Descent from the Cross after Raphael. Their shared narrative and related figure organization support a derivative/adaptive comparison. The paired view makes alteration and new handling part of the answer, rather than equating adaptation with mechanical reproduction.

headings: Module 6: European Print and Indian Bazaar
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Calcutta Art Studio Buddha and the Agra print introduce two uses of reproducible imagery: devotional circulation and a published architectural view. headings: Indigenous Painting practices and Printmaking
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Kali/Tara, the Calcutta Art Studio Buddha and the Pune Mahavir print form a sequence of studio devotional images. Different religious subjects use reproducible colour imagery and commercial publication. The significant distinction is between the regional subject, the technology and the agency of the producing studio.

headings: Indigenous Painting practices and Printmaking
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The lithographed book cover, tiger-shaped script and hawk-shaped script compare writing as readable content and constructed image. The grouping connects text, animal outline and circulation rather than treating the animal forms as natural-history studies.

name: Kali and Tara — Calcutta Art Studio

sections.Process: Course reading: The lecture attributes the colour print to Calcutta Art Studio. The article’s External Checks documents the sheet as a chromolithograph.
sections.Edition & Circulation: Course reading: Names in multiple scripts and studio/copyright lines appear on the bottom margin, making the sheet a published devotional commodity.
sections.Composition & Motifs: The sheet is split vertically into two goddess images. Kali at left has four arms, loose dark hair, a garland of heads, a blade and severed head, with reclining bodies below. Tara at right carries a lotus, blade and bowl-like object. A skull garland, skull crown, tiger-skin garment and snakes distinguish her. Flames rise on both sides of Tara’s feet, with a pale reclining body beneath. A loose skull and bones appear along the lower left.
sections.Subject Matter vs Technique Origin: Course reading: Bengali religious iconography is reproduced through a modern colour-print enterprise.

lecture_notes.text: A single print depicting both goddesses. The caption cites the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

claims.text: The lecture attributes the colour print to Calcutta Art Studio.
The article’s External Checks documents the sheet as a chromolithograph.
The sheet is split vertically into two goddess images.
Kali at left has four arms, loose dark hair, a garland of heads, a blade and severed head, with reclining bodies below.
Tara at right carries a lotus, blade and bowl-like object.
A skull garland, skull crown, tiger-skin garment and snakes distinguish her.
Flames rise on both sides of Tara’s feet, with a pale reclining body beneath.
A loose skull and bones appear along the lower left.
Names in multiple scripts and studio/copyright lines appear on the bottom margin, making the sheet a published devotional commodity.
Bengali religious iconography is reproduced through a modern colour-print enterprise.

confidence_tiers.3: Unsupported external fact; consolidated attribution note.

significance.religious/cosmological: Course reading: The paired arrangement invites comparison of related but distinct goddess iconographies.
significance.economic/trade: Course reading: Studio imprint and copyright text mark a commercial printed image.
significance.visual/aesthetic: Course reading: Shading and atmospheric backgrounds coexist with frontal iconographic clarity.

distinctions.claim: Kali and Tara are identical repetitions of one goddess made by hand-colouring a monochrome sheet.
distinctions.why_wrong: Kali and Tara are not interchangeable labels for one repeated figure; compare attributes, garlands, ground and body treatment.

name: Relief, intaglio and planography

sections.Definition: Course reading: Relief prints from raised ink-bearing areas. Intaglio prints from recessed lines or areas. Planography separates image and non-image areas on a substantially flat surface, as in lithography.
sections.Nearest Confusable Terms: Course reading: Woodcut is relief. Engraving and etching are intaglio. Lithography is planographic. The surface carrying ink, not the subject or colour, determines the basic category.
sections.Applied To: Course reading: The Sebastian matrix/impression and relief demonstration illustrate raised surfaces. The colonial engravings illustrate intaglio. The stone and diagrams introduce lithography.

headings: Indigenous Printing in the Indian subcontinent
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The unfinished Pedana woodblocks and finished Polavaram cotton connect a carved matrix to textile printing. This precedes the European Saint Sebastian block-and-impression pair. The sequence compares a printing principle across supports and uses, while keeping the specific practices distinct.

headings: Types of Printmaking
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Saint Sebastian woodblock and its impression are paired to make relief printing legible as a transfer process. Raised and cut-away areas relate to printed and unprinted areas. The following lithographic demonstration shows a different printing principle, so all reproducible images cannot be grouped as woodcuts.

headings: Types of Printmaking
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The lithographic stone demonstration and relief-printing video compare planographic and raised-surface printing. Matrix, inking and transfer provide the distinctions. The subsequent landscape prints show how reproducible processes serve published views, rather than making process and subject the same category.

headings: Types of Printmaking
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The lithographic stone demonstration and relief-printing video compare planographic and raised-surface printing. Matrix, inking and transfer provide the distinctions. The subsequent landscape prints show how reproducible processes serve published views, rather than making process and subject the same category.

headings: Types of Printmaking
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Sicri Gully and Salsette temple prints are followed by the Antiquities of India title page. Views, maker credits and antiquarian publication framing connect Indian sites with a British audience. Pictorial composition and the date of a published plate remain separate from the date of a visit or monument.

headings: Indigenous Painting practices and Printmaking
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Bombay scene and Annoda Prosad Bagchi’s Vijaya pair different makers and subjects within the print economy. They follow the book and calligraphic prints and precede studio devotional sheets. The comparison expands the field of print production beyond a single colonial publisher or one religious audience.

name: Chromolithography and hand-colouring

sections.Definition: Course reading: Chromolithography produces colour through successive lithographic printings, requiring alignment. Hand-colouring adds colour manually to an existing impression. A work may combine them.
sections.Nearest Confusable Terms: Course reading: A colour woodcut is not a chromolithograph. A hand-tinted chromolithograph is not a contradiction. Misregistration concerns alignment of printed components, not every irregular edge of applied colour.
sections.Applied To: Course reading: Buddhadeb and Hawk are captioned chromolithographs. Vijaya is hand-tinted chromolithography. Scene in Bombay uses etching, aquatint and hand-colouring.

name: Misregistration — analytical study term

sections.Definition: Course reading: Misregistration is unintended misalignment between successive printed components, often visible where one colour shifts relative to another or to a key outline. This term is added from the corpus brief.
sections.Nearest Confusable Terms: Course reading: Hand-colouring outside a line, paper distortion, photographic blur and image-compression fringes can resemble misregistration but have different causes.
sections.Applied To: Course reading: The colour-print examples in Modules 6 and 7 provide contexts for asking how successive printed components align. The term is supplied as an analytical study concept by the corpus brief.

claims.text: Misregistration is unintended misalignment between successive printed components, often visible where one colour shifts relative to another or to a key outline.

The colour-print examples in Modules 6 and 7 provide contexts for asking how successive printed components align.

name: European Print and Indian Bazaar

sections.Argument: Course reading: Printmaking changes knowledge circulation and popular culture while indigenous workshops select technologies, develop imagery and create markets. The module moves from colonial documentation toward local devotional and social imagery.
sections.Evidence & Artworks: Course reading: Landscape engravings, Solvyns’s people and market, Roxburgh’s plant plate, Kalighat–Battala comparisons and Calcutta/Pune studios establish different purposes and production systems.
sections.Course Throughline: Course reading: Imported processes do not determine subject matter or authorship. Local makers transform reproducible images into regional cultural forms.

headings: Module 6: European Print and Indian Bazaar
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Calcutta Art Studio Buddha and the Agra print introduce two uses of reproducible imagery: devotional circulation and a published architectural view. The Agra credits separate sketch, drawing and engraving. European print technology and South Asian subjects therefore require separate statements about medium, audience and labour.

headings: Indigenous Printing in the Indian subcontinent
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The unfinished Pedana woodblocks and finished Polavaram cotton connect a carved matrix to textile printing. This precedes the European Saint Sebastian block-and-impression pair. The sequence compares a printing principle across supports and uses, while keeping the specific practices distinct.

headings: Types of Printmaking
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Sicri Gully and Salsette temple prints are followed by the Antiquities of India title page. Views, maker credits and antiquarian publication framing connect Indian sites with a British audience. Pictorial composition and the date of a published plate remain separate from the date of a visit or monument.

headings: Print and Colonial Documentation of People, Places and Plants in the Indian Subcontinent
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Solvyns’s potters and bazaar, the Kanaree cave view and Roxburgh’s botanical plate form a sequence of people, places and plants under colonial documentation. Each image organizes knowledge differently. The grouping asks who observes, draws, commissions and publishes, as well as what is represented.

headings: Indigenous Painting practices and Printmaking
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The broom scene and cat-with-lobster Kalighat painting are followed by the cat motif in a Battala print. Social commentary and a recognizable subject pass between painting and print. The repeated cat is therefore a comparison of pictorial treatment and circulation, not evidence that the two objects share one manufacturing process.

name: Under the Wave off Kanagawa — The Great Wave

sections.Process: Course reading: Japanese colour woodblock print: relief printing uses aligned impressions from carved blocks.
sections.Edition & Circulation: Course reading: The module treats Japanese prints as portable objects collected and reinterpreted in Europe.
sections.Composition & Motifs: The enormous wave curls from upper left over three narrow boats with bent rowers. White foam branches like claws, while tiny snow-topped Fuji sits near the lower centre of the distant horizon. A title cartouche and signature occupy upper left.
sections.Subject Matter vs Technique Origin: Course reading: Japanese landscape and labour are represented through Japanese printmaking. Later European responses may borrow composition while using other media.

name: Courtesan after Eisen — Van Gogh

sections.Composition: A copied tall figure is enclosed in a bright yellow inner rectangle. An added outer field contains water, reeds, birds and other creatures.
sections.Palette & Pigment: Strong yellow, red, blue and green replace the original’s more restricted tones. Conspicuous strokes animate the background.
sections.Line & Hand: Thick dark contours and visibly separated strokes translate the print’s linear structure into painting.
sections.Motifs & Hidden Details: Long-legged birds stand at left, lily pads and flowers run down the water margin, and a frog-like creature occupies the bottom centre. The dragon robe motif is retained but coarsened into painted colour.

name: Portrait of Père Tanguy

sections.Composition: The seated frontal man forms a broad central triangle with folded hands. Japanese images cover the wall behind him, cropping around his shoulders and hat.
sections.Palette & Pigment: Blue-green coat, warm face and bright yellow-orange background contrast through separate directional strokes.
sections.Line & Hand: Short strokes model the face and jacket, unlike the flatter reproduced prints behind him.
sections.Motifs & Hidden Details: A mountain image appears above the hat. Female figures flank both shoulders and the lower-right edge. Floral imagery occupies the lower left.
sections.Subject Matter vs Technique Origin: Course reading: A French sitter is painted by Van Gogh among Japanese images: collecting becomes part of portraiture rather than proof the sitter is Japanese.

occurrences.argument: Course reading: Père Tanguy’s Japanese-print backdrop is followed by Sunflowers and Almond Blossoms under Van Gogh’s imagined Japan. headings: Why Reclaiming the Ocean and Oceanic Ties is Important Today?
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Vijaya Vitthala warrior, Ascetic Riding a Nag and Père Tanguy form the final recap. Stone carving, a marbled painting and a European portrait surrounded by Japanese prints supply three different histories of connection. Reclaiming oceanic ties means attending to those mechanisms of encounter and agency rather than treating regions as visually isolated.

name: Portrait of Émile Zola

sections.Composition: Zola sits at left with an open illustrated book, turned toward a desk crowded with papers and books. A Japanese-style screen stands at far left. Three reproduced pictures occupy the upper-right wall.
sections.Palette & Pigment: A dark suit and wall contrast with pale pages and face. The reproductions create lighter inset rectangles.
sections.Text–Image Relationship: Books and reproductions characterize the sitter’s intellectual and artistic associations.
sections.Motifs & Hidden Details: The screen includes a small bird on a flowering branch. A feather quill rises from an ornamental desk vessel. A blue booklet visibly bears Manet’s name. The wall grouping contains Olympia, a Japanese standing figure and a partly obscured monochrome group.

claims.text: Zola sits at left with an open illustrated book, turned toward a desk crowded with papers and books.
A Japanese-style screen stands at far left.
Three reproduced pictures occupy the upper-right wall.
The screen includes a small bird on a flowering branch.
A feather quill rises from an ornamental desk vessel.
A blue booklet visibly bears Manet’s name.
The wall grouping contains Olympia, a Japanese standing figure and a partly obscured monochrome group.
A dark suit and wall contrast with pale pages and face.
The reproductions create lighter inset rectangles.
Books and reproductions characterize the sitter’s intellectual and artistic associations.

name: Water Lilies — Art Institute example

sections.Composition: Floating pads and blossoms gather around a large open blue patch of reflected water. No sky horizon or shore anchors the view.
sections.Perspective Convention: The viewer looks down at water while reflections imply vertical surroundings. Surface and depth remain deliberately ambiguous.
sections.Palette & Pigment: Cool blue and green dominate with small pink-white flowers.
sections.Line & Hand: Broken, overlapping touches define pads, flowers and blue-green-violet reflections.

lecture_notes.text: Left. The caption cites the Art Institute of Chicago.

headings: Van Gogh, the search of sunlight and “Japan” in Arles, France, 1888
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Art Institute Water Lilies and MoMA’s multi-panel work compare related subject matter at different scales. The gallery arrangement adds seating, open floor and viewing distance to the painted surface. Compare individual works and the bodily viewing conditions rather than treating every Water Lilies image as one object.

name: Camille Monet in Japanese Costume — La Japonaise

sections.Composition: A turning woman in a long red robe fills the canvas while round fans scatter across the wall and floor. The robe’s train curves across the foreground.
sections.Figural Style: The woman looks back toward the viewer and raises an open fan. Her light hair contrasts with the theatrical Japanese garment.
sections.Motifs & Hidden Details: An embroidered warrior with sword occupies the robe’s lower front. Birds and plants cover the upper red fabric. Fans contain miniature landscapes and figures.
sections.Subject Matter vs Technique Origin: Course reading: A European sitter performs a fashionable imagined Japan through costume and collected objects in a European painting.

lecture_notes.text: Left. Shown alongside Cassatt’s The Letter and a Japanese print.

headings: Van Gogh, the search of sunlight and “Japan” in Arles, France, 1888

The three illustrate different forms of Japanese reception. Cassatt’s intaglio medium remains distinct from woodblock, and Mizuno’s later print cannot be her direct source.

headings: Van Gogh, the search of sunlight and “Japan” in Arles, France, 1888
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Hokusai’s Mannen Bridge and Monet’s Japanese bridge are paired through the bridge’s graphic curve. name: Japonisme — appreciation, collecting and appropriation

sections.Definition: Course reading: In this module, Japonisme names European engagement with Japanese art, especially prints: collecting objects, copying images and adapting cropping, pattern, contour and spatial organization.
sections.Nearest Confusable Terms: Course reading: Ukiyo-e is a Japanese pictorial tradition, not the name for its European reception. Orientalism asks broader questions about representing and idealizing an imagined East. Aesthetic influence does not always entail a change of medium.
sections.Applied To: Course reading: Eisen–Van Gogh is a direct source comparison. Cassatt–Mizuno and Hokusai–Monet are parallel comparisons whose chronology and media must remain distinct.

headings: Module 7: Wave of Japonisme
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Great Wave, the introductory ukiyo-e image and Lake Chuzenji establish a Japanese print vocabulary of framing, flat colour, landscape and scale. They prepare the following Van Gogh–Eisen comparison. The Japanese examples remain distinct works rather than interchangeable illustrations of one national style.

headings: An Introduction to Ukiyo-e
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Eisen’s courtesan and Van Gogh’s painted version present a direct source-and-adaptation pair. Figure and costume are retained while palette, border imagery and medium change. The next Père Tanguy portrait extends appropriation into collecting and assembling Japanese images within a European painting.

headings: Artist’s Imagination and Idealisation of Japan
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Père Tanguy’s Japanese-print backdrop is followed by Sunflowers and Almond Blossoms under Van Gogh’s imagined Japan. Collecting, colour, contour and cropped plant forms offer different ways to engage Japanese imagery. Japanese influence is therefore broader than a Japanese subject or the direct copy of one print.

headings: Van Gogh, the search of sunlight and “Japan” in Arles, France, 1888
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Père Tanguy’s Japanese-print backdrop is followed by Sunflowers and Almond Blossoms under Van Gogh’s imagined Japan. headings: Van Gogh, the search of sunlight and “Japan” in Arles, France, 1888
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Zola’s portrait and the enlarged reproductions on its wall make artistic association visible inside an interior. Olympia, a Japanese figure and a monochrome group are objects of pictorial reference within Manet’s painting. The components connect collecting to portrait identity without becoming separately inspected original prints.

headings: Van Gogh, the search of sunlight and “Japan” in Arles, France, 1888
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Jane Avril and Divan Japonais place Japanese-inspired cropping and contour within Parisian entertainment publicity. Performer, spectator and instrument are organized differently in the two posters. Their subject and lithographic process remain distinct from Japanese woodblock manufacture.

headings: Van Gogh, the search of sunlight and “Japan” in Arles, France, 1888
occurrences.argument: Course reading: La Japonaise, Cassatt’s The Letter and Mizuno’s After the Bath compare costume performance, domestic pictorial design and a Japanese print. The three illustrate different forms of Japanese reception. Cassatt’s intaglio medium remains distinct from woodblock, and Mizuno’s later print cannot be her direct source.

headings: Van Gogh, the search of sunlight and “Japan” in Arles, France, 1888
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Hokusai’s Mannen Bridge and Monet’s Japanese bridge are paired through the bridge’s graphic curve. The populated urban crossing and garden pond have different scales, settings and media. The comparison makes a formal relation explicit without establishing that Monet copied this exact impression.

name: Asia in Amsterdam — entrance and gallery arrangements

sections.Physical Arrangement: At the entrance, large exhibition lettering fills a deep blue wall at right. Two decorated cylindrical objects occupy stepped blue niches along the route. An enlarged harbour scene covers the rear-left wall, with a floral hanging visible beyond it. In the smaller gallery view, a narrative tapestry spans the left wall, two tall glass cases stand on the floor, and framed pictures run along the right wall toward a doorway. In the long gallery, cabinets and textiles line the left, still-life paintings line the right, and central cases, paired tall vessels and a rear screen establish an axis under the skylight. The nearest right-hand still life visibly includes a blue-and-white ewer.
sections.What the Arrangement Communicates: Course reading: Placing functional luxury objects beside pictures of luxury goods lets the viewer compare circulating material things with their painted representations. Sightlines between rooms extend that comparison beyond isolated cases. The quoted review asks how Asian imports shaped Dutch identity. That argument is distinct from the physical description.
sections.Objects & Origins: Course reading: Asia in Amsterdam, Rijksmuseum, 2015–16, is the captioned exhibition. The review mentions Bouke de Vries’s concluding works.

name: Belitung cargo — bowls arranged as waves around a dhow

sections.Physical Arrangement: Dozens of bowls tilt upward on slender transparent rods at graduated heights. The rods build a wave-like crest at right and lower troughs in front. A model sailing dhow sits centrally behind the foreground bowls, with visitors visible beyond the enclosure. The close view shows repeated but varied brown painted bowl designs.
sections.What the Arrangement Communicates: Course reading: Repetition makes cargo quantity and serial production visible. The undulating heights and model ship restore an image of maritime transport. This is a curatorial reconstruction, not the recovered archaeological arrangement.
sections.Objects & Origins: Course reading: The lecture describes Chinese Tang-period cargo from a merchant dhow wrecked near Belitung around 830, exhibited in Singapore. The model is interpretive display furniture. It is not the excavated hull.

name: Sleeping Cupid above paper boats — Lampedusa display

sections.Physical Arrangement: The framed Caravaggio hangs high in a dark blue wall recess under focused light. Numerous small folded paper boats spread irregularly across the floor beneath, separated from visitors by a low rope. A large vertical interval divides painting and boats.
sections.What the Arrangement Communicates: Course reading: The elevated painting and scattered paper boats connect historical art with a Mediterranean setting. The museum’s trust-and-dialogue title gives this vertical juxtaposition a contemporary social reading.
sections.Objects & Origins: Course reading: Caravaggio’s Eros of 1608 is captioned within the Lampedusa 2016 exhibition. The floor objects belong to the installation context.

lecture_notes.text: Right photograph, paper boats arranged on the floor beneath Eros. The caption identifies the painting and exhibition.

headings: Understanding interconnections, mass production and social life of objects through maritime history
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The reclining beach figure, Caravaggio’s Sleeping Cupid and the painting’s placement above paper boats connect bodily vulnerability with a Mediterranean exhibition setting. Height and floor placement make the comparison specific. The paper boats belong to the display, and the beach figure remains a separate work rather than a view of Caravaggio’s painted figure.

name: The Cross — Subodh Kerkar

sections.Subject & Narrative: A cross with widening arm ends is densely encrusted with shells. Its recognizable outline survives while the surface becomes irregular and organic.
sections.Iconographic Attributes: The cross is a Christian form. No corpus of Christ is attached in this view.
sections.Material & Technique: Pale cupped shells accumulate over a dark substrate, with several larger white shells below the crossing. The slide asks about collaboration with the ocean.
sections.Architectural Placement: Photographed on a plain pale wall, then repeated as The Oceanic Cross in a Museum of Goa video card.

occurrences.argument: Course reading: Belitung bowls arranged as waves around a dhow are compared with underwater documentation and Kerkar’s encrusted cross. The museum uses repeated cargo to give production and shipping a spatial form; the underwater image records another stage of the objects’ lives. The cross introduces the ocean’s material participation in contemporary making.

headings: Collaborating with the Ocean for making Artwork?
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Kerkar’s cross and the Museum of Goa title card develop the question of collaborating with the ocean. Encrustation, the cross form and its documentation connect material change to a recognizable cultural sign. This moves beyond the Belitung display’s reconstruction of past shipping into present artistic agency.

name: The Ship of Tarshish — Prasad Raghavan

sections.Subject & Narrative:
A boat-shaped sculptural hull carries a rectangular stack of small container-like boxes.

Course reading: Its title connects a contemporary cargo form with the lecture’s Biblical trade discussion.
sections.Iconographic Attributes: The title is written on the hull. Container forms make modern logistics visible.
sections.Material & Technique: Constructed installation with a dark angular hull and repeated box modules.
sections.Architectural Placement: The work stands inside a long rough-walled hall with repeated windows and exposed roof structure. The hull’s pointed end projects toward the viewer.

historical_context_as_indexed: Ship of Tarshish, Biblical Ties and Trade

lecture_notes.text: Right. Installation paired with a photograph of Vallarpadam container terminal. Image courtesy of Robert E. D’Souza.

headings: Ship of Tarshish, Biblical Ties and Trade
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Raghavan’s container-ship work connects the Biblical Tarshish reference with contemporary shipping under Biblical Ties and Trade. It follows the street campaign and precedes Tallur’s tile installation. The sequence makes historical narrative, current commerce and local material history different ways of reclaiming global ties.

name: Oceanic history and connected art histories

sections.Argument: Course reading: The lecture places art history alongside histories of the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean, naming Braudel, K. N. Chaudhuri and Ashin Das Gupta. It asks how political, social and cultural networks can organize the study of art.
sections.Evidence & Artworks: Course reading: Trade-textile exhibitions, shipwreck cargo and contemporary installations supply cases of movement, serial production and changing object lives.
sections.Course Throughline: Course reading: The ocean connects production, exchange, display and interpretation. It is both a historical route and an active contemporary medium.

headings: Module 8: Reclaiming the Ocean
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Ahmedabad exhibition poster frames its title with a floral trade-textile detail. The original cloth becomes the visual identity of a contemporary exhibition about distant markets. The ensuing museum sequence examines how present displays assemble evidence for those historical connections.

headings: Module 8: Reclaiming the Ocean

headings: Museum practice, curation and recent exhibitions on historical oceanic networks
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Interwoven Globe entrance banner and gallery sightline connect an exhibition’s public framing with its arrangement of textiles and images. Position, scale and the view through the gallery invite cross-object comparisons. The next Asia in Amsterdam installation provides a second curatorial method for presenting historical circulation.

headings: Asia in Amsterdam: The Culture of Luxury in the Golden Age
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Asia in Amsterdam places imported Asian goods near paintings that represent luxury consumption, with vessels and furniture in cases and textiles or pictures on walls. The entrance image and successive gallery views make trade visible through juxtaposition. A painting of a vessel and an exhibited vessel have complementary evidential roles.

headings: When Indian Flowers Bloomed in Distant Lands
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Mumbai trade-textile graphic, ROM display and Southeast Asian Ramayana textile connect contemporary curatorial framing with different uses of Indian cloth. Their sequence distinguishes an exhibition identity, an arranged group of garments and an individual ceremonial textile. Market, subject and present display are different parts of its social history.

headings: Understanding interconnections, mass production and social life of objects through maritime history
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Belitung bowls arranged as waves around a dhow are compared with underwater documentation and Kerkar’s encrusted cross. The museum uses repeated cargo to give production and shipping a spatial form; the underwater image records another stage of the objects’ lives. The cross introduces the ocean’s material participation in contemporary making.

headings: Understanding interconnections, mass production and social life of objects through maritime history
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Belitung bowls arranged as waves around a dhow are compared with underwater documentation and Kerkar’s encrusted cross. headings: Collaborating with the Ocean for making Artwork?
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Kerkar’s cross and the Museum of Goa title card develop the question of collaborating with the ocean. Encrustation, the cross form and its documentation connect material change to a recognizable cultural sign. This moves beyond the Belitung display’s reconstruction of past shipping into present artistic agency.

headings: Ship of Tarshish, Biblical Ties and Trade
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Raghavan’s container-ship work connects the Biblical Tarshish reference with contemporary shipping under Biblical Ties and Trade. It follows the street campaign and precedes Tallur’s tile installation. The sequence makes historical narrative, current commerce and local material history different ways of reclaiming global ties.

headings: Mangalore Terracotta Tiles and Swiss-German Christian Connections (1865 onwards)
occurrences.argument: Course reading: Tallur’s seated figure with a log is paired with Veni, vidi, vici’s passage between banks of roof tiles. Bodily encounter and material transformation connect the works, while their arrangements remain distinct. The Mangalore tile heading brings mission-industry history into the contemporary installation.

headings: Archaeological Excavation in Elephanta and Colonial Legacy Reimagined
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The framed elephant image is placed in relation to Quintessential’s screen, sculptural objects and fragmented forms. Under the Elephanta and colonial-legacy heading, archival representation and contemporary installation rework historical authority. Precise spatial relationships supply the curatorial argument, not the mere fact that several objects share a room.

headings: Why Reclaiming the Ocean and Oceanic Ties is Important Today?
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Vijaya Vitthala warrior, Ascetic Riding a Nag and Père Tanguy form the final recap. Stone carving, a marbled painting and a European portrait surrounded by Japanese prints supply three different histories of connection. Reclaiming oceanic ties means attending to those mechanisms of encounter and agency rather than treating regions as visually isolated.

claims.text: The lecture connects a contemporary biennale and its local public campaign to Kochi/Muziris’s longer trade histories.
Artworks bring Biblical, industrial and colonial connections into present exhibition space.
Street posters, Raghavan’s container ship, Tallur’s tile environment and Quintessential address different scales of connection.
Regional identity is represented through outward connections and contested histories, not through isolation.

confidence_tiers.3: Unsupported external fact; consolidated attribution note.

headings: Why Reclaiming the Ocean and Oceanic Ties is Important Today?
occurrences.argument: Course reading: The Vijaya Vitthala warrior, Ascetic Riding a Nag and Père Tanguy form the final recap. Stone carving, a marbled painting and a European portrait surrounded by Japanese prints supply three different histories of connection. Reclaiming oceanic ties means attending to those mechanisms of encounter and agency rather than treating regions as visually isolated.
